text: This Advanced UI Lab combines everything from this chapter in one real build: a Close All Tasks UI Action on the Change Request form from Chapter 4's lab, finished with a GlideModal confirmation and a shared UI Script, rather than two separate pieces built in isolation.

Step one is the shared UI Script, DateFormatHelpers, holding one function, formatShortDate. It guards against an empty date by returning a fallback string, then builds a short month, day, and year string from a real Date object. This lives in its own standalone record, not copy-pasted into either script that will end up calling it.

Step two is the UI Action's client script. It reads the open task count and the change's created date off the form, calls formatShortDate from the shared UI Script to build a confirmation message, then opens a GlideModal titled Close All Related Tasks. The onPromptComplete preference is a callback that fires with the user's confirm or cancel choice — only when the user actually confirms does the script call gsftSubmit, which re-submits the form carrying an action name the server-side script is watching for.

Step three is the server-side script, and it only runs after that confirmed submit, never on the first click. It queries the task table for every active task whose parent is the current change record, closes each one by setting its state to Closed Complete, and adds an info message once finished. Cancel the dialog instead, and this entire block of server code never executes at all.

Step four shows the real payoff of extracting that date logic into a UI Script in the first place. A completely separate, unrelated Client Script elsewhere on the same form also needs to display that created date. It includes the same DateFormatHelpers UI Script and calls the identical formatShortDate function — one definition, two independent callers, and one single place to fix a bug if the date format ever needs to change.

This lab is really Chapter 7 compressed into one scenario — pick the lightest API that actually fits the job, GlideModal over GlideDialogWindow for a simple confirmation, and the moment logic repeats anywhere on the form, extract it into a shared UI Script rather than copy-pasting it a second time. Next up: Chapter 8 begins with Lesson 31, building a Scripted REST API to expose your application's data beyond the UI entirely.
